## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Indasamānagottajātaka* (Ja 161, PTS J II 41–43) is a canonical Jātaka tale situated in the second book (*Dukanipāta*, *Dalhavagga*) of the collection [Fausböll 1879; Sahni 2008]. According to the narrative framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the story while residing at Jetavana regarding a headstrong monk (*dubbacajātika*), noting that the monk had similarly met his death in a past existence due to stubbornness and refusal to heed the counsel of the wise [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), an ascetic from the Indasamāna clan kept an elephant as a pet, completely disregarding the warnings of his teacher, the Bodhisatta [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. When the elephant grew mad and destructive, it trampled the obstinate ascetic to death [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Sahni 2008]. The central moral is encapsulated in verse urging disciples to choose their associates carefully and shun company with fools: *Māssu bālena sangañchi, dukkho bālehi sangamo* ("Do not have fools for companions, suffering comes from mixing with fools") [Anandajoti 2010]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the unteachable ascetic is identified as the obstinate monk and the leader of the ascetic company as the Buddha [Fausböll 1879].

Textual reuse data computed by DharmaNexus demonstrates extensive correspondence between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus detects cross-language alignments with verses preserved in the Tibetan versions of the *Udānavarga* (D4099 and D0326) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].
